opus-5.5.text:
That's a fair question, and I'd say I'm moderately confident about the mechanism but more cautious about the quantitative details.

The core idea is fairly general. Language has a hierarchical, roughly compositional structure, and the statistical correlations between tokens decay with distance. A model with a finite amount of data can only detect correlations that rise above the sampling noise. So as you increase the training set, the range over which the model can reliably use context grows, and it can resolve deeper levels of the hierarchy. That gives you a scaling law, and in a sense an effective context length that depends on the data.

Why do I believe this extends beyond what we tested? The argument doesn't depend on a particular window size. It depends on how correlations decay and how fast you can estimate them. As long as that decay behaves similarly at longer ranges, the same logic should hold.

But there are real reasons for caution. First, at long ranges, natural text may not follow the same decay. Document-level structure, narrative, and code with long dependencies could behave quite differently from the local statistics we measured. Second, our empirical checks used fairly modest models and datasets. At frontier scale, architecture and optimization effects might start to matter in ways our simplified picture ignores. Third, the hierarchical models we analyze are idealizations. Real language is messier, with overlapping structures, not just a clean tree.

So I'd frame it this way: the theory makes a falsifiable prediction. If you measure how token correlations decay at longer distances in a given corpus, you should be able to predict how the benefit of more context scales with data. I'd be delighted if someone tested that at much longer context lengths. If it breaks, that would tell us something interesting about what the simple picture is missing.

r001.rationale: It says that increasing the training set expands the range of context the model can reliably use.

r002.rationale: It does not identify approximately 50 tokens as the tested context scale.

r003.rationale: It expresses caution about extending the theory beyond tested ranges, but does not specify contexts of roughly three or four sentences.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not very confident, and I think that's the right epistemic stance given what we actually did. Let me explain what the theory does and where the extrapolation gets dangerous.

The core idea is that language has a hierarchical, compositional structure, and we modeled it with a generative grammar, essentially a tree where tokens at the leaves are produced by latent variables higher up. In that picture, the model has to learn correlations between tokens at increasing distances, and the key result is that the amount of data needed to resolve a correlation at distance ell grows as a power of ell. Deeper levels in the hierarchy are harder to learn because the signal that tells you about a latent variable high up is diluted across many tokens below it. That gives you a scaling law where the test loss decays as a power law in the number of training samples, and the exponent is set by the branching factor and the depth of the grammar.

Now, the context length enters in two ways. First, within the model, the context limits how far the correlations you can exploit extend. If your context is shorter than the scale of some latent structure, you simply can't learn it, and the loss plateaus at a level set by that missing information. Second, in our experiments on real data, we only tested up to contexts of a few hundred to a couple thousand tokens, and we see the prediction hold in that range: longer contexts bring in more levels of structure, and the loss keeps decreasing with a consistent exponent.

So where could it break? The strongest assumption is that the hierarchy keeps going. Our grammar is self-similar, every level looks like every other level, and that's what gives a clean power law. Real text is clearly not self-similar across all scales. At the level of a sentence, you have syntax, which is quite tree-like. At the level of a paragraph or a document, you have discourse structure, topics, arguments, and I would not bet that these obey the same branching statistics. Beyond that, at the scale of a whole book or a corpus, I honestly don't know what the structure looks like, and there's a real possibility that correlations saturate or change character entirely. If that happens, the exponent would change, or you'd see a crossover to a different regime, and our theory as stated wouldn't predict where.

The second concern is that at very long contexts, the bottleneck may no longer be data at all. It may be optimization, or architectural, how attention actually manages to route information across tens of thousands of tokens. Our theory is really a statement about the statistics of the data and what a well-trained model can in principle extract. It's agnostic about whether gradient descent on a transformer gets there, and I think at long range that gap matters more.

What I would say in favor of the theory is that it makes a falsifiable prediction. If you measure the mutual information between tokens as a function of distance in real text, our picture says it should decay as a power law, and we actually did measure that and it looks reasonably consistent out to the distances we checked. So the honest answer is: I'd put real money on the mechanism, that hierarchical structure is what drives the scaling, and much less money on the specific exponent extending to a hundred thousand tokens. If someone showed me a measurement of that mutual information at those scales, that would update me much more than any theoretical argument I could make.

astra-6.text: I would be cautious about that. The agreement in the regime we tested gives us some confidence, but it doesn’t establish that the same scaling will hold at much longer context lengths. That’s an extrapolation, and it depends on whether the assumptions behind the theory remain valid. So I would treat it as a prediction to test, rather than something we’ve already demonstrated.

sol-6.1.text: I would distinguish confidence in the mechanism from confidence in the extrapolation. We tested a finite range of context lengths, so I wouldn’t claim that this establishes the theory at arbitrarily long contexts. The question is whether the assumptions that explain the scaling in that range continue to hold. If longer contexts introduce a different regime, then the prediction could change. So I’d treat the extension as a testable prediction, and I’d want measurements at substantially longer contexts before making a strong claim.
